Brass
bras
n. (a copper alloy; the metal of the outer court and of judgment; rendering Hebrew nechosheth, Greek chalkos)
From the Saxon braes. The Hebrew nechosheth more strictly denotes copper or bronze, the Authorized Version's brass covering the whole family of copper alloys; the same consonants give nachash, a serpent, and the pun is unmistakable in the brasen serpent Moses lifted up.

Biblical Definition

Brass in Scripture is the metal of the outer court and so of judgment borne. Gold belongs to the holy place, where God dwells; brass belongs to the altar and the laver, where sin is dealt with before a man may go further in — the arrangement is theological before it is architectural. The most striking use is the remedy in the wilderness: “And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived” (Numbers 21:9), which our Lord makes the express type of his own lifting up. The judgment-metal is shaped into the very image of the curse, and the dying are healed by looking. Brass also figures the hardness of a heaven shut in judgment: “thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass” (Deuteronomy 28:23), the covenant curse for disobedience. Paul uses it for religious noise without love — “I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1) — the metal that resonates loudly and contains nothing. And John sees the glorified Christ with “feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace” (Revelation 1:15), the Judge standing on the metal of judgment.

Webster 1828 Definition

Copper alloy; in the tabernacle the metal of the outer court, the altar, and the laver — hence the metal of judgment borne. Moses' serpent of brass is the type of Christ lifted up.

expand to see more

BRASS, n. [Sax. braes.] An alloy of copper and zinc, of a yellow color; in Scripture usually copper or bronze.

2. Impudence; a brazen face — a figurative use.

3. In the tabernacle, the metal of the altar of burnt offering, the laver, and the court vessels.

4. A figure of hardness or of a heaven shut up; as, thy heaven shall be brass, Deut. 28.

5. In Scripture, of the serpent lifted up in the wilderness, Num. 21; of the feet of the glorified Christ, Rev. 1.

Key Scripture

Numbers 21:9 — "And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived."

Deuteronomy 28:23 — "And thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass, and the earth that is under thee shall be iron."

1 Corinthians 13:1 — "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal."

Revelation 1:15 — "And his feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace; and his voice as the sound of many waters."

Modern Corruption

Tabernacle metals are read as decoration or as ancient technology, and their teaching is lost. Scripture assigns them by station — brass at the altar, gold in the holiest — and the assignment preaches the way of approach to God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss is one of typological literacy rather than doctrinal attack. A reader who takes the metals as furnishing detail will skim Exodus and Leviticus as inventory, when in fact the gradient from brass to gold as one moves from court to holy place to holiest is a diagram of atonement: judgment must be met at the brasen altar and cleansing at the brasen laver before there is any question of the golden furniture within.

The principle to recover is the one our Lord himself drew from this metal. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up — and the type is exact at the point most people miss. The remedy was made in the form of the curse itself, a brass serpent for serpent-bitten men, just as he who knew no sin was made sin for us. The dying Israelite was not asked to fetch anything or do anything; he was asked to look. That is why 1 Corinthians 13:1 stings: brass can also be all sound and no substance, and a religion of noise without love has the metal without the meaning.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nechosheth is copper or bronze, sharing consonants with nachash, serpent; nachush means brazen or hard. Greek chalkos is copper or brass, and chalkolibanon is the fine burnished brass of Revelation 1:15.

expand to see more

Hebrew nechosheth (H5178) — copper, bronze, brass; the metal of the altar and the laver.

Hebrew nachash (H5175) — serpent; the wordplay behind the brasen serpent of Numbers 21.

Hebrew nechushtan (H5180) — the name Hezekiah gave the serpent when he broke it as an idol.

Greek chalkos (G5475) — copper, brass, money; the sounding brass of 1 Corinthians 13:1.

Greek chalkolibanon (G5474) — fine brass, burnished as in a furnace; the feet of the glorified Christ.

Usage

"Of the type of Christ lifted up: when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived (Numbers 21:9)."

"Of a heaven shut in covenant judgment: thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass (Deuteronomy 28:23)."

"Of loud religion without love: I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal (1 Corinthians 13:1)."
